facts.claim: Garrett Kato wrote "Sweet Jane". It is track 4 on That Low and Lonesome Sound and runs 3:20.
The 2018 release is listed as August 10, 2018 on Nettwerk Music Group. The album first came out in September 2015, and Discogs lists that edition as a self-released CD.
Audiomack's metadata for the song credits Anthony Lycenko as producer. The track is listed as © Garrett Kato under exclusive license to Nettwerk Music Group Inc.

Album credits on Discogs name Garrett Kato as producer and as player of guitar, banjo, piano, synth, bass, organ and vocals. Anthony Lycenko is credited with recording and mixing, Ben Livermore with drums and percussion, Jamie Birrel with bass, and Hayle Marie and Mimi Gilbert with vocals.
Lyric-site credits for this song list Ben Livermore on drums and percussion, Hayley Marie on harmonies, and Garrett Kato on guitars, vocals, bass and banjo.
The album was recorded in Byron Bay, NSW, Australia. Locations were Kato's garage, his home studio and 301 Studios. It was mastered by Kathy Naunton.
The album was two years in the making. Kato recorded most songs multiple times, saying he kept adjusting them and tending to them like a garden.
Kato said the album is about his move from Canada to Australia and letting go of a past life. He called it basically a personal diary of manhood and letting go.

Kato is a Canada-born, Australia-based singer-songwriter and producer. He has worked with Julia Stone, Tones and I and Riley Pearce, and has played shows with Damien Rice and Ziggy Alberts. His later albums are Hemispheres (2020) and Small Town Rituals (2022).
Around the 2015 release Kato opened for Pete Murray on a 27-date Australian tour. He named Bob Dylan and Kendrick Lamar among the musicians who inspire him.

research.lineage: Sweet Jane sits in the Australian-based singer-songwriter tradition of dreamy, low-key acoustic pop and folk, with an overtly southern-leaning style described by one interviewer.

draft:
A grieving person usually goes one of two ways: they feel too much, or they shut it all off. **Sweet Jane** is about the second kind, and about watching it happen to someone you love. Garrett Kato's narrator isn't the one in trouble. He's the one standing nearby, noticing that Jane has gone numb. The chorus puts it plainly: her heart "don't wanna be working right," and she's in a bad enough place that "Now you tried everything / Just to feel something." There's no scolding in it. It reads like a diagnosis spoken by a friend who has run out of ways to help.

The song never says outright what put her there, but the second half points to it. Her father has told her he'll be "re-made / Into a spirit that lives inside your mind," which sounds like comfort offered in the face of an ending. Jane won't take it. She turns down the reasons anyone lives and dies and settles on a flat fact instead: rivers just run into the ocean. It's a bleak kind of peace, and the narrator doesn't argue with it. Earlier, the image of a home where she "once stayed" that has washed away in the rain does the same quiet work. Something is already gone, and the song is set in the time just after.

What makes it bearable is how gently Kato handles it. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls under everything, bright and steady. Sustained bass notes and a soft kick and snare keep the slow tempo from drifting. Kato's voice is breathy and close, and the harmonies (credited to Hayley Marie) fold in tight around him, so the lines about numbness come out warm instead of cold. The room sounds small and clean. That fits the album's origins: it was cut in Byron Bay, in Kato's garage, his home studio and 301 Studios, recorded and mixed by Anthony Lycenko, with Ben Livermore on drums. Kato spent two years on the record, recording songs over and over and, in his words, tending to them like a garden. You can hear that care in how little gets in the way.

Kato has described the album as a diary of his move from Canada to Australia and of letting go of a past life. **Sweet Jane** fits that story from an angle. It's a song about someone else's letting go, sung by someone who has done his own. The tone is the low-key, slightly southern-leaning acoustic folk that runs through the record, unhurried and sure of itself.

The song ends where the chorus has been heading all along, on "nothing left to lose," and the narrator's best line is the simplest: "Oh, my thoughts are still with you." He can't fix her, and he says so by staying.

**Sweet Jane** sticks because it lets you feel what it's like to love someone through their numbness: you can't reach them, so you keep your voice soft and stay close anyway.

factCheck.note: The words match the lyric, but the quote budget is three lines. Turned into a paraphrase.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: 'Now you tried everything / Just to feel something'
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly, and it is two consecutive lines.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: 'Oh, my thoughts are still with you'
Lyric quote: 're-made / Into a spirit that lives inside your mind'
factCheck.note: The lyric reads 'spirt', and the quote budget was exceeded. Paraphrased the father's lines instead of quoting.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quotes 'once stayed' and 'nothing left to lose'
factCheck.note: These pushed the review past three quoted lines. Paraphrased. The imagery they describe (home washed away in the rain) is in the lyrics.

factCheck.note: The lyrics' structure shows the final repeated stanza, so the closing is supported. 'Second half' was softened to 'later verses'.

factCheck.claim: Fingerpicked acoustic guitar, bright and steady
factCheck.note: Fingerpicked acoustic guitar is supported by all three passes. 'Bright' appears in only one pass, so it was dropped.

factCheck.claim: Sustained bass notes and a soft kick and snare; slow tempo
factCheck.note: Bass and kick/snare are backed by two passes, and the slow tempo by all three. 'Soft' appeared in only one pass, so the drums are now described as simple.

factCheck.claim: Kato's voice is breathy and close
factCheck.note: All three passes say breathy, and two say intimate. Kato is credited with vocals.

factCheck.claim: Harmonies fold in tight, credited to Hayley Marie

factCheck.note: Changed to clean and intimate, which two or more passes support.
